cards.statement: WCAG guidelines provide the pass-or-fail checks used to decide conformance.
cards.explanation: Success criteria provide the testable requirements. Guidelines state the broader goals rather than individual pass-or-fail checks.
cards.misconception: The guidelines themselves are the testable conformance requirements.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: WCAG 2 Layers of Guidance

cards.statement: WCAG Level AA conformance requires meeting Level A as well as Level AA success criteria.
cards.explanation: Level AA builds on Level A; it is not a separate checklist that replaces the lower level.

source.title: Understanding Conformance

cards.statement: WCAG permits authors to exclude an inaccessible sidebar when evaluating the rest of a page for conformance.
cards.explanation: Conformance applies to a complete page. Authors cannot declare a selected region conformant while excluding an inaccessible sidebar.
cards.misconception: A conforming main region makes the surrounding page conformant.

source.title: Understanding Conformance

cards.statement: WCAG assesses conformance across the pages of a checkout process, including its payment step.
cards.explanation: Every page needed to complete a process must meet the target level. An accessible opening step does not cover a later nonconforming step.

source.title: Understanding Conformance

cards.statement: WCAG allows a conforming alternate version to use a different technology from the original page.
cards.explanation: An alternate version may use different technology while providing equivalent information and functionality in the same language and staying equally current.

source.title: Understanding Conformance: Conforming Alternate Versions

cards.statement: WCAG recommends Level AAA conformance as a general policy for entire websites.
cards.explanation: WCAG advises against a blanket Level AAA policy for entire sites because some content cannot satisfy every Level AAA success criterion.
cards.misconception: Level AAA is the recommended universal conformance target for whole websites.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

cards.statement: The WCAG Techniques document prescribes the implementations developers use to achieve conformance.
cards.explanation: Techniques provide informative implementation options. Developers may use another approach that demonstrably meets the relevant success criteria.
cards.misconception: Conformance requires implementing one of the published Techniques.

source.title: Understanding Techniques for WCAG Success Criteria

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, a success criterion's position within its guideline indicates its conformance level.
cards.explanation: WCAG 2.2 appends new criteria to preserve existing numbering. The printed level, rather than position within the guideline, identifies the conformance level.
cards.misconception: Criteria remain ordered by conformance level within each guideline.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: Numbering in WCAG 2.2

cards.statement: Publishing WCAG 2.2 left WCAG 2.1 and 2.0 in place as current W3C Recommendations.
cards.explanation: WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede WCAG 2.0 or 2.1, so content can still conform to those earlier versions as current Recommendations.

source.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

cards.statement: WCAG 3.0 has W3C Recommendation status alongside WCAG 2.2.
cards.explanation: WCAG 3.0 is a W3C Working Draft, not a completed Recommendation. Its draft status means the proposed requirements are still under development.
cards.misconception: The published WCAG 3.0 document is already a finalized W3C standard.
cards.volatilityNote: WCAG 3.0 may advance to a different publication status after this check.

source.title: W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, a focused control partly covered by a sticky footer passes Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA).
cards.explanation: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (Level AA) addresses author-created content that entirely hides a control receiving keyboard focus. Partial overlap is permitted.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.4.11: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) belongs to the Level AA conformance requirements.
cards.explanation: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) is Level AAA. Its enhanced protection is outside the requirements for a Level AA target.
cards.misconception: The enhanced focus-obscuring criterion is part of Level AA.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.4.12: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Focus Appearance (Level AAA) compares the same indicator pixels in focused and unfocused states.
cards.explanation: Focus Appearance (Level AAA) measures a 3:1 contrast change at the same pixels between states, rather than comparing the indicator with its adjacent color.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.4.13: Focus Appearance

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Dragging Movements (Level AA) accepts a keyboard shortcut as the alternative to dragging.
cards.explanation: Dragging Movements (Level AA) needs a non-dragging single-pointer route unless an exception applies. A keyboard shortcut alone does not provide that route.
cards.misconception: A keyboard alternative satisfies the pointer-specific dragging requirement.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.5.7: Dragging Movements

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) applies its 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum to links in sentences.
cards.explanation: Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts targets in sentences, or targets whose size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text.
cards.misconception: Inline links in prose are subject to the same minimum target dimensions as standalone controls.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Consistent Help (Level A) requires repeated help mechanisms to keep their relative page order.
cards.explanation: Consistent Help (Level A) concerns order relative to other content across a set of pages in the same page variation. User-initiated changes are excepted.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.2.6: Consistent Help

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) accepts password-manager support as a mechanism.
cards.explanation: Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) lists password-manager support as assistance that reduces memory demands during password entry.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.8: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA) includes an Object Recognition exception.
cards.explanation: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA) retains the Alternative and Mechanism exceptions. Object recognition is not an exception at this level.
cards.misconception: The enhanced authentication criterion exempts object-recognition tests.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.9: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, the 44 by 44 CSS pixel criterion Target Size (Enhanced) forms part of Level AA conformance.
cards.explanation: Target Size (Enhanced) is Level AAA in WCAG 2.2. Its 44 by 44 CSS pixel threshold does not belong to a Level AA conformance target.
cards.misconception: The 44 by 44 CSS pixel target-size requirement is Level AA.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.5.5: Target Size (Enhanced)

cards.statement: In WCAG 2.2, 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed because assistive technology now relies on browsers to parse HTML.
cards.explanation: Assistive technology used to parse markup itself. Many issues that once failed Parsing now fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value instead.

source.title: Understanding SC 4.1.1: Parsing (Obsolete and removed)

cards.statement: Browsers build the accessibility tree from the DOM for use by assistive technology.
cards.explanation: The accessibility tree represents semantic information such as names, descriptions, roles and states, rather than being a visual copy of the page.

source.title: Accessibility tree - MDN Web Docs Glossary

cards.statement: Browsers give `Details` the implicit link role when exposing it to assistive technology.
cards.explanation: An `a` element needs `href` for its implicit link role. The shown markup has an implicit generic role.
cards.misconception: The anchor tag supplies link semantics even when its href attribute is absent.

source.title: ARIA in HTML

cards.statement: A `<section aria-label="Details">` element exposes a region landmark to assistive technology.
cards.explanation: A section becomes a region landmark when it has an accessible name, allowing assistive technology to identify that page region.

source.title: ARIA: region role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<header>` inside an `<article>` supplies the document's implicit banner landmark.
cards.explanation: A header nested inside article content does not receive the implicit banner role. The banner mapping is for the page-level header, subject to the nesting restrictions.
cards.misconception: A header is a banner landmark regardless of its enclosing sectioning content.

source.title: ARIA: banner role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The `<search>` element gives its contents the semantics of an editable search input.
cards.explanation: The search element is a landmark container for search or filtering functionality. Authors place the actual input controls inside it.
cards.misconception: The search container has the semantics of a search input control.

source.title: <search>: The generic search element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Browsers derive a native heading's level from the depth of its surrounding `<section>` elements.
cards.explanation: A native heading gets its implicit level from the number in its h1–h6 tag. Nesting it in sections does not change that implicit level.
cards.misconception: The depth of section nesting determines the implicit accessibility level of a native heading.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, and h6

cards.statement: Meaningful Sequence (Level A) permits different reading orders that preserve the content's meaning.
cards.explanation: Meaningful Sequence (Level A) needs a correct reading order to be programmatically determinable when order affects meaning. Independent articles may support more than one correct order.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.3.2: Meaningful Sequence

cards.statement: HTML allows two visible `<main>` elements on one page when each has a unique accessible label.
cards.explanation: A document may have only one main element without the hidden attribute, so a label cannot make a second visible main valid.
cards.misconception: A unique accessible label lets a page repeat the main landmark the way it can repeat nav or region landmarks.

source.title: <main>: The Main element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<caption>` inside a data table supplies a programmatically associated title for that table.
cards.explanation: The caption identifies its parent table and provides a table-specific title that assistive technology can use.

source.title: <caption>: The Table Caption element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: For a button with valid `aria-labelledby` and `aria-label`, browsers use the `aria-label` value as its name.
cards.explanation: When aria-labelledby resolves to usable naming text, it takes precedence over aria-label. Supplying both does not give aria-label priority.
cards.misconception: A direct aria-label string outranks an aria-labelledby reference.

source.title: ARIA: aria-labelledby attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<label>` element's `for` value links it to a form control's `name` attribute.
cards.explanation: An explicit HTML label associates through the control's id, matched by the label's for value. The control's name attribute is not the matching target.
cards.misconception: The label for value targets the control's form-submission name.

source.title: <label>: The Label element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: In HTML-AAM, a text input's name falls back to `placeholder` after the earlier naming sources fail.
cards.explanation: HTML-AAM places placeholder after title in the text-input name computation. This specifies a fallback source rather than guaranteeing consistent spoken output.
cards.volatilityNote: HTML-AAM remains a Working Draft; this card tests its published computation, not universal assistive-technology behavior.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: Text Input Accessible Name Computation

cards.statement: On a button, `aria-label` appends its text to the name supplied by the button's content.
cards.explanation: If aria-label is set on a button, its value replaces the name the button would get from its content; the content is hidden from assistive technology users rather than appended.
cards.misconception: aria-label supplements rather than replaces the button's content-derived name.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions: Naming with a String Attribute Via aria-label - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: `aria-label` on a plain `<div>` with its implicit generic role gives that div a valid accessible name.
cards.explanation: The generic role prohibits accessible naming. Adding aria-label to a plain div is not a valid way to name it under that role.
cards.misconception: aria-label is valid as a naming mechanism on elements with any implicit role.

source.title: ARIA: generic role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG recommends visible interface text as the first choice for an accessible name.
cards.explanation: The APG prioritizes names derived from visible text. Keeping naming text visible makes incorrect or stale labels easier to notice and maintain.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG calls for translating `aria-label` strings along with the rest of a localized interface.
cards.explanation: aria-label contains human-readable naming text. The APG says these strings need translation alongside the rest of the interface.

source.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) requires link text to explain its purpose independently of surrounding content.
cards.explanation: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) allows link text together with programmatically determined context to establish the purpose, such as the containing paragraph.
cards.misconception: Level A link purpose has to be clear from the isolated link text.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context)

cards.statement: Headings and Labels (Level AA) evaluates semantic markup rather than the wording of headings.
cards.explanation: Headings and Labels (Level AA) evaluates whether headings and labels describe their topic or purpose. Correct semantic markup is a separate concern.
cards.misconception: This criterion tests structural markup instead of descriptive wording.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.4.6: Headings and Labels

cards.statement: Label in Name (Level A) permits extra words around the visible label text in an accessible name.
cards.explanation: Label in Name (Level A) requires the name to contain the visible label text. Placing that text at the start is a best practice, not a requirement.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.5.3: Label in Name

cards.statement: MDN's first rule of ARIA favors a suitable native HTML element over a custom ARIA equivalent.
cards.explanation: When HTML already provides the needed semantics and behavior, MDN directs authors to use that native feature instead of recreating it with ARIA.

source.title: ARIA - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: WAI-ARIA 1.2 lets authors use abstract roles as general-purpose roles for custom widgets.
cards.explanation: Abstract roles organize the specification's role hierarchy. WAI-ARIA prohibits authors from assigning them to elements in page content.
cards.misconception: Abstract roles are fallback choices for custom controls that lack a more specific role.

source.title: Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2: Abstract Roles

cards.statement: `aria-valuenow` is a global ARIA property, like `aria-label` and `aria-describedby`.
cards.explanation: aria-valuenow is role-specific: WAI-ARIA 1.2 uses it on range roles such as slider, spinbutton and scrollbar, while aria-label and aria-describedby are global.
cards.misconception: ARIA value properties are global attributes that work independently of the element's role.

source.title: Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2: Global States and Properties

cards.statement: ARIA in HTML permits `role="heading"` on a native `<button>` used as a section title.
cards.explanation: ARIA in HTML disallows role="heading" on button. The button retains native functionality that conflicts with the expectations of a heading.
cards.misconception: An explicit ARIA role is valid on a native element whenever it describes the author's intended use.

source.title: ARIA in HTML: Avoid overriding interactive elements with non-interactive roles

cards.statement:
With `

Details

`, browsers retain "Details" in the accessibility tree.
cards.explanation: The presentation role removes the heading semantics from this h2, while its text remains available to assistive technology.

source.title: ARIA: presentation role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Browsers continue displaying visible content when authors add `aria-hidden="true"` to its element alone.
cards.explanation: aria-hidden changes exposure to assistive technology, not visual rendering. Hiding the element on screen takes a separate visual-hiding mechanism.

source.title: ARIA: aria-hidden attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Authors can expose text inside an `aria-hidden="true"` ancestor by adding `aria-hidden="false"` to its span.
cards.explanation: A descendant's aria-hidden="false" does not override an ancestor's aria-hidden="true". The ancestor continues to exclude that text from the accessibility tree.
cards.misconception: A descendant can opt back into the accessibility tree by overriding its ancestor's aria-hidden value.

source.title: ARIA: aria-hidden attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Name, Role, Value (Level A) applies to a custom control assembled from scripted HTML elements.
cards.explanation: Script-generated controls fall within Name, Role, Value (Level A). Their control semantics need to be available programmatically to assistive technology.

source.title: Understanding SC 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value

cards.statement: W3C publishes WAI-ARIA 1.3 as a Working Draft while its requirements remain under development.
cards.explanation: WAI-ARIA 1.3 has Working Draft status, so it is not a completed W3C Recommendation. Its proposed requirements remain subject to revision.
cards.volatilityNote: WAI-ARIA 1.3 may advance to a different publication status after this check.

source.title: Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.3

cards.statement: Browsers give `<div role="button">` Enter-key activation through its ARIA role.
cards.explanation: role="button" supplies semantics, not keyboard activation. Authors implement the key handling for a custom div button.
cards.misconception: Assigning the button role makes the browser provide native button keyboard behavior.

source.title: ARIA: button role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A button already in the tab sequence stays there when its author sets `aria-disabled="true"` alone.
cards.explanation: aria-disabled communicates an unavailable state without changing focusability. This lets authors keep an unavailable control discoverable through keyboard navigation.

source.title: ARIA: aria-disabled attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG toggle-button pattern changes the label from "Mute" to "Unmute" when the pressed state changes.
cards.explanation: An APG toggle button keeps its label stable across pressed states. The state communicates whether the named action is on or off.
cards.misconception: A toggle button's label changes to describe the opposite action whenever its pressed state changes.

source.title: Button Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, `aria-pressed="mixed"` marks a toggle button whose controlled items hold differing values.
cards.explanation: aria-pressed is tri-state: true, false or mixed. Mixed means the items the button controls do not all share the same value; the default, undefined, means the element is not a toggle.

source.title: ARIA: aria-pressed attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG disclosure pattern places `aria-expanded` on the button that reveals and hides the content.
cards.explanation: In the disclosure pattern, the controlling button carries aria-expanded. Its value describes whether that button's associated content is currently open.

source.title: Disclosure (Show/Hide) Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG tabs pattern names its `tabpanel` elements through `aria-labelledby` references to their tabs.
cards.explanation: The tabpanel's aria-labelledby reference associates the panel's accessible name with its tab. Users can identify which tab's content the panel represents.

source.title: Tabs Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: In the APG tabs pattern, `aria-selected="true"` belongs on the displayed `tabpanel` element.
cards.explanation: The APG puts aria-selected="true" on the active tab, not its panel. The other tabs carry aria-selected="false".
cards.misconception: The displayed panel carries the selected state instead of the tab that selects it.

source.title: Tabs Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: In the APG menu pattern, Escape returns focus from an open submenu to the item that opened it.
cards.explanation: The APG uses Escape to dismiss the menu containing focus and restore focus to its launching context. For a submenu, that context is its parent menu item.

source.title: Menu and Menubar Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: For typical site navigation with expandable link groups, the APG points authors to the disclosure pattern over menubar.
cards.explanation: The APG navigation menubar example opens with a caution: menubar needs complex functionality that typical site navigation does not, and the disclosure pattern suits it better.

source.title: Navigation Menubar Example - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG presents its widget examples as verified for mobile and touch interaction in production interfaces.
cards.explanation: The APG does not indicate mobile or touch compatibility for its examples. Authors still need interoperability testing before using the example code in production.
cards.misconception: The APG verifies that its example widgets work with mobile and touch interaction before authors adopt them.
cards.volatilityNote: The APG's mobile and touch compatibility guidance may change as its examples and testing coverage evolve.

source.title: Read Me First - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Keyboard (Level A) exempts a handwriting-based text field from providing a keyboard method of entering text.
cards.explanation: Keyboard (Level A) bases its exception on the underlying function. Entering text can use keystrokes, even when the interface also offers handwriting recognition.
cards.misconception: A path-dependent input technique makes the underlying text-entry function exempt from keyboard access.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.1.1: Keyboard

cards.statement: No Keyboard Trap (Level A) calls for instructions when a component uses a nonstandard keyboard exit.
cards.explanation: No Keyboard Trap (Level A) allows a nonstandard keyboard escape method if users receive instructions. The instructions explain how to move focus out of the component.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.1.2: No Keyboard Trap

cards.statement: Character Key Shortcuts (Level A) accepts a letter-key shortcut active only while its component has focus.
cards.explanation: Character Key Shortcuts (Level A) permits shortcuts confined to the focused component. Alternatives are letting users disable the shortcut or remap it to include a non-printable key.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.1.4: Character Key Shortcuts

cards.statement: In the APG keyboard model, pressing Tab moves focus from one menu item to the next within the same menu.
cards.explanation: The APG uses arrow keys for movement within composite widgets and Tab for movement between components. Tab does not step through a menu's items.
cards.misconception: Composite menus use the same item-by-item Tab navigation as an ordinary series of links.

source.title: Developing a Keyboard Interface - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Browsers place `tabindex="0"` elements in the sequential focus order according to their document order.
cards.explanation: tabindex="0" adds an element to sequential keyboard navigation at its position in document order. It does not assign the element a higher priority.

source.title: tabindex HTML global attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Bypass Blocks (Level A) permits a skip link that becomes visible when keyboard focus reaches it.
cards.explanation: A skip link may appear on focus rather than remain permanently visible. Revealing it on focus lets sighted keyboard users find and use the bypass mechanism.

source.title: Adding a link at the top of each page that goes directly to the main content area

cards.statement: The HTML definition of `tabindex` classifies positive values as invalid for sequential keyboard navigation.
cards.explanation: Positive tabindex values are valid, but MDN discourages them because they impose an explicit navigation priority that makes keyboard order harder to maintain.
cards.misconception: Positive tabindex values are invalid HTML rather than valid values that guidance discourages.

source.title: tabindex HTML global attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: By default, browsers follow the CSS `order` values of flex items when they move keyboard focus with Tab.
cards.explanation: Flexbox order changes only the visual rendering. Tabbing and speech order follow the source order, so CSS reordering can separate what users see from where focus goes.
cards.misconception: Changing the visual order of flex items also changes their order for keyboard focus.

source.title: Ordering flex items - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Browsers restrict matching of the CSS `:focus-visible` selector to focus initiated through a physical keyboard.
cards.explanation: Browsers use heuristics for :focus-visible, including whether the control expects keyboard input. A text input may match after a pointer click.
cards.misconception: :focus-visible is a strict detector of physical-keyboard input rather than a heuristic for showing focus.

source.title: :focus-visible CSS pseudo-class - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: An author can move focus to a rendered heading with `tabindex="-1"` by calling its `focus()` method.
cards.explanation: tabindex="-1" makes the heading a programmatic focus target without adding it to the Tab sequence. This enables deliberate focus placement on static content.

source.title: tabindex HTML global attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: In roving tabindex navigation, `focus()` keeps the current scroll position by default for off-screen targets.
cards.explanation: The browser scrolls the newly focused item into view during roving tabindex navigation. This is a built-in benefit of moving DOM focus between items.
cards.misconception: Programmatic focus changes in a roving tabindex widget leave scrolling entirely to the application.

source.title: Developing a Keyboard Interface - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG's recommended multi-select listbox model selects an option when unmodified arrow keys move focus to it.
cards.explanation: In the APG's recommended multi-select listbox model, unmodified arrow keys move focus while preserving selection. Navigation and selection are distinct actions.
cards.misconception: Moving focus through a multi-select listbox necessarily selects the newly focused option.

source.title: Listbox Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Calling `showModal()` on a dialog makes the rest of its document inert through browser behavior.
cards.explanation: showModal() makes elements outside the dialog and its descendants inert within the same document. A modal inside an iframe does not block the surrounding document.

source.title: HTMLDialogElement: showModal() method - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: By default, browsers let Escape close an HTML dialog opened with `showModal()`.
cards.explanation: Native modal dialogs provide Escape dismissal through the browser. Authors get this behavior without adding their own Escape-key handler.

source.title: <dialog> HTML dialog element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Browsers prioritize the first focusable dialog child over a later focusable child marked `autofocus`.
cards.explanation: A focusable dialog child marked autofocus overrides the usual first-focusable-element choice when the browser places initial focus.
cards.misconception: The first focusable element in document order outranks an explicit autofocus target inside a dialog.

source.title: <dialog> HTML dialog element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: The APG suggests initially focusing the least destructive action when a dialog confirms an irreversible change.
cards.explanation: For a final step that is difficult to undo, the APG advises considering the least destructive action as the initial focus target, such as Cancel in a deletion confirmation.

source.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: The APG permits a dialog to return focus to a different element when the workflow makes that target more logical.
cards.explanation: The APG normally returns focus to the opener. Another target can fit when the opener is gone or a directly related next step makes returning to it unnecessary.

source.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

cards.statement: Authors can enforce background blocking on a custom dialog by setting `aria-modal="true"`.
cards.explanation: aria-modal describes modality to assistive technology; it does not implement it. A custom dialog's code must prevent interaction with background content.
cards.misconception: Declaring a custom dialog modal through ARIA makes the browser enforce its interaction boundary.

source.title: ARIA: aria-modal attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: MDN recommends `tabindex="-1"` on the `<dialog>` element to make a native modal keyboard-accessible.
cards.explanation: MDN explicitly says not to put tabindex on the dialog element. Focus management within a native dialog does not call for adding that attribute to its container.
cards.misconception: A native dialog needs a negative tabindex on its container to support keyboard focus management.

source.title: <dialog> HTML dialog element - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Browsers keep an `inert` subtree available in the accessibility tree for reading with assistive technology.
cards.explanation: Inert content is excluded from the accessibility tree. Its text is unavailable through ordinary assistive-technology reading, not merely removed from keyboard navigation.
cards.misconception: inert stops interaction while keeping the subtree exposed for assistive-technology reading.

source.title: inert HTML global attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Error Identification (Level A) requires authors to describe an automatically detected input error in text.
cards.explanation: Error Identification (Level A) calls for text that identifies the affected input and describes the error, helping users understand what went wrong.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.1: Error Identification

cards.statement: A text field's `aria-label` alone satisfies Labels or Instructions (Level A) for users reading the screen.
cards.explanation: Labels or Instructions (Level A) calls for guidance presented to users. An aria-label supplies naming text for assistive technology, rather than a visible label or instruction.
cards.misconception: An accessible name alone supplies the guidance that this criterion expects users to perceive.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.2: Labels or Instructions

cards.statement: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA) requires a confirmation page before a user submits a payment.
cards.explanation: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA) permits reversible submissions, checks with correction, or review and confirmation. A confirmation page is one option.
cards.misconception: Covered financial submissions need a confirmation page even when another permitted safeguard exists.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.3.4: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)

cards.statement: A select that opens another page on change passes On Input (Level A) when instructions placed before it warn users.
cards.explanation: On Input (Level A) accepts a change of context on selection when users are advised before using the control, for example by instructions placed ahead of the select.

source.title: Understanding SC 3.2.2: On Input

cards.statement: Setting `aria-required="true"` alone makes the browser automatically block an empty text input's form submission.
cards.explanation: On supported native controls, required participates in HTML constraint validation. aria-required communicates a requirement to assistive technology and adds no validation behavior.
cards.misconception: aria-required activates the browser's native missing-value validation.

source.title: ARIA: aria-required attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A `<legend>` within a `<fieldset>` gives related form controls a shared group label.
cards.explanation: fieldset groups related controls, and its legend identifies the group, such as an address type. This gives the controls a shared context beyond their individual labels.

source.title: Grouping Controls - WAI Forms Tutorial

cards.statement: A clear placeholder can replace a text field's visible label under MDN's accessibility guidance.
cards.explanation: MDN advises using placeholder text as a brief hint, rather than a label replacement. The hint disappears as users enter a value, so it cannot preserve the field's identifying guidance.
cards.misconception: A sufficiently clear placeholder is an acceptable substitute for a field label.

source.title: placeholder HTML attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Authors can meet Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) for eligible HTML fields with suitable `autocomplete` tokens.
cards.explanation: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) accepts suitable autocomplete tokens as purpose metadata for eligible fields. These tokens communicate the kind of personal information the user enters.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose

cards.statement: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) includes a field where users enter another person's birthday.
cards.explanation: Identify Input Purpose (Level AA) covers listed input purposes when fields collect information about the user. A field for another person's birthday falls outside that scope.
cards.misconception: A listed input purpose falls within this criterion even when the field collects another person's data.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose

cards.statement: MDN advises authors to defer `aria-invalid="true"` for an empty required field until form submission.
cards.explanation: For a required field, MDN advises setting aria-invalid="true" in response to validation, rather than merely because the initial value is empty.

source.title: ARIA: aria-invalid attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: WAI-ARIA 1.2 lets user agents expose `aria-errormessage` for a control with `aria-invalid="false"`.
cards.explanation: An aria-errormessage relationship is pertinent when aria-invalid="true". User agents must suppress that relationship when aria-invalid is false.
cards.misconception: The error-message relationship remains exposed regardless of the control's validity state.

source.title: WAI-ARIA 1.2: aria-errormessage property

cards.statement: The WAI images tutorial gives `alt=""` to a photo whose content the adjacent text already describes.
cards.explanation: The tutorial treats a picture already described by adjacent text as decorative, so an empty alt stops the same information being announced twice.

source.title: Decorative Images - WAI Images Tutorial

cards.statement: ARIA in HTML maps the decorative markup `` to the presentation role.
cards.explanation: The empty alt in this markup marks the image as decorative. ARIA in HTML assigns presentation semantics to this case because the image has no other naming source.

source.title: ARIA in HTML

cards.statement: HTML-AAM names `` "Summary".
cards.explanation: HTML-AAM takes an image's name from nonempty alt ahead of title. The title attribute supplies a fallback name when the alt attribute is absent.
cards.misconception: An image's title attribute overrides a supplied alt when computing its accessible name.
cards.volatilityNote: HTML-AAM is a Working Draft; its published image-name computation may change.

source.title: HTML Accessibility API Mappings 1.0: img Accessible Name Computation

cards.statement: The WAI tutorial recommends "Printer icon" as the alternative for an image that serves as a Print button.
cards.explanation: A functional image's alternative identifies its action or destination, such as "Print". Describing the object alone misses the control's purpose.
cards.misconception: A functional image needs an alternative describing the pictured object rather than the action it performs.

source.title: Functional Images - WAI Images Tutorial

cards.statement: The WAI tutorial treats a chart's short identifying `alt` as a sufficient alternative to its detailed data.
cards.explanation: WAI pairs a short description identifying a complex image with a longer text equivalent of its essential information, including important data and relationships.
cards.misconception: A short chart identifier conveys the detailed information needed for a complex image's alternative.

source.title: Complex Images - WAI Images Tutorial

cards.statement: Authors may treat an informative CSS background image as exempt from Non-text Content (Level A).
cards.explanation: Non-text Content (Level A) covers meaningful visual information regardless of how the author inserts it. CSS backgrounds need an equivalent way to convey that information.
cards.misconception: Rendering meaningful information as a CSS background removes the text-alternative obligation.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.1.1: Non-text Content

cards.statement: Authors can give an inline SVG graphic an accessible name through its child `<title>` element.
cards.explanation: In the name computation, an SVG title element is a host-language text alternative, so it supplies the accessible name of its parent graphic.

source.title: Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2: Host Language Label

cards.statement: A heading image with matching alt text fails Images of Text (Level AA) when CSS could style real text the same way.
cards.explanation: When the technologies in use can achieve the same visual presentation, Images of Text asks for real text. Alt text is no exception; only Customizable and Essential are.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.5: Images of Text

cards.statement: For an image CAPTCHA, Non-text Content (Level A) treats a purpose label as a complete text-alternative solution.
cards.explanation: For CAPTCHA, Non-text Content (Level A) requires purpose-identifying text plus alternative CAPTCHA forms using different sensory modes, accommodating different disabilities.
cards.misconception: Identifying a CAPTCHA's purpose fulfills the criterion without providing alternative sensory forms.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.1.1: Non-text Content

cards.statement: Authors can replace synchronized captions with a transcript under Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A).
cards.explanation: Captions (Prerecorded) (Level A) calls for synchronized captions for prerecorded audio in video. A separate transcript lacks that synchronization; clearly labeled media alternatives for text are excepted.
cards.misconception: A separate transcript is interchangeable with synchronized captions for this criterion.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.2.2: Captions (Prerecorded)

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) sets a 4.5:1 floor for paragraph text outside its exceptions.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) compares text with its background. Meeting the threshold helps users with reduced contrast sensitivity read the text.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)

cards.statement: Under Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA), bold text qualifies as large-scale based on font weight alone.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) uses both weight and size: at least 14 point for bold text or 18 point for other text, or equivalent sizes for CJK fonts.
cards.misconception: Bold font weight makes text eligible for the large-scale category regardless of its size.

source.title: WCAG 2.2: Large-scale text definition

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) uses unrounded computed ratios when authors assess text contrast.
cards.explanation: Threshold comparisons use the computed ratio's full precision. Rounding a result for display does not make a below-threshold contrast ratio pass.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)

cards.statement: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts the text of a logo whose colors follow its brand identity.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts logo text whose appearance follows the brand identity. The Understanding guidance excludes low contrast added as an author's styling choice.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)

cards.statement: Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA) applies its 7:1 threshold to large-scale text as well as body text.
cards.explanation: Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA) sets 7:1 for ordinary text and 4.5:1 for large-scale text. Large text has its own threshold.
cards.misconception: The enhanced threshold for ordinary text also applies to large-scale text.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.6: Contrast (Enhanced)

cards.statement: Non-text Contrast (Level AA) sets 3:1 for an active checkbox's state mark when authors style that mark.
cards.explanation: Non-text Contrast (Level AA) evaluates the mark needed to recognize a checkbox state against adjacent colors. The requirement concerns visual identification, not decorative parts.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast

cards.statement: Authors may use hue alone to distinguish success from failure under Use of Color (Level A).
cards.explanation: Use of Color (Level A) calls for another visual cue, such as text or a symbol, when hue communicates a status. Users need a way to identify that status beyond hue.
cards.misconception: Distinct hues are sufficient to communicate which status represents success and which represents failure.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.1: Use of Color

cards.statement: Resize Text (Level AA) lets authors use browser zoom for the 200 percent text enlargement requirement.
cards.explanation: Resize Text (Level AA) allows browser zoom when users can double text size without losing content or functionality. Captions and images of text are exceptions.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.4: Resize Text

cards.statement: Reflow (Level AA) bases its narrow-layout test on a device's physical screen width of 320 pixels.
cards.explanation: Reflow (Level AA) uses 320 CSS pixels for vertically scrolling content, rather than hardware pixels. Content needing a two-dimensional layout, such as a data table, is excepted.
cards.misconception: The reflow width refers to physical screen pixels rather than CSS viewport pixels.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.10: Reflow

cards.statement: Text Spacing (Level AA) tests a page's initial CSS spacing rather than the effects of user spacing changes.
cards.explanation: Text Spacing (Level AA) checks for lost content or functionality when users apply the specified spacing overrides. It does not dictate the page's default spacing.
cards.misconception: The criterion checks authors' default spacing rather than resilience to user-specified spacing.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.12: Text Spacing

cards.statement: Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA) requires authors' hover popups to stay visible as the pointer enters them.
cards.explanation: The Hoverable condition in Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA) supports moving the pointer onto the added content, for example to inspect a tooltip with magnification.

source.title: Understanding SC 1.4.13: Content on Hover or Focus

cards.statement: A disabled button's label remains subject to the text threshold in Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA).
cards.explanation: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) exempts text that is part of an inactive user interface component. A disabled button's label falls under the Incidental exception.
cards.misconception: Text in a disabled control follows the contrast threshold for text in active controls.

source.title: WCAG 2.2: Contrast (Minimum)

cards.statement: A screen reader may announce changes in an `aria-live="off"` region while focus is inside that region.
cards.explanation: MDN describes off as limiting update announcements to a region that contains focus. The precise spoken behavior depends on the browser and assistive technology.
cards.volatilityNote: Actual announcements depend on evolving browser and assistive-technology behavior.

source.title: ARIA live regions - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, the `status` role gives its updates the implicit `aria-live="assertive"` priority.
cards.explanation: WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives status an implicit aria-live="polite" value. Its default priority suits advisory updates rather than urgent interruptions.
cards.misconception: The status role requests assertive live-region handling by default.

source.title: ARIA: status role - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: A countdown marked up with the `timer` role carries an implicit `aria-live` value of polite.
cards.explanation: WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives the timer role an implicit aria-live value of off, so authors who want its updates announced as they happen set aria-live themselves.
cards.misconception: A timer implicitly requests polite live-region handling for its changing value.

source.title: WAI-ARIA 1.2: timer role

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, `aria-atomic="true"` has assistive technology present a changed live region as a whole.
cards.explanation: aria-atomic="true" instructs assistive technology to include the region's full content, rather than just the changed portion. It controls the scope of an update presentation.

source.title: ARIA: aria-atomic attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: By default, `aria-relevant` includes removal events among the live-region changes marked for notification.
cards.explanation: aria-relevant defaults to "additions text", covering added nodes and text changes. Authors include "removals" or "all" when they want deletions treated as relevant.
cards.misconception: Removing content counts as a relevant live-region update under the default aria-relevant setting.

source.title: ARIA: aria-relevant attribute - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: MDN recommends creating a live region before authors insert the update they want announced.
cards.explanation: Declare the live region before an update and give assistive technology time to register it. MDN calls inclusion in the initial markup the most reliable approach.
cards.volatilityNote: Live-region registration and update announcements vary as browsers and assistive technologies evolve.

source.title: ARIA live regions - MDN Web Docs

cards.statement: Status Messages (Level AA) expects authors to automatically focus messages so assistive technology detects updates.
cards.explanation: Status Messages (Level AA) requires programmatic identification that lets assistive technology present a status update without moving focus. Taking focus is not the mechanism it specifies.
cards.misconception: A status announcement depends on moving keyboard focus to the updated message.

source.title: Understanding SC 4.1.3: Status Messages

cards.statement: A Stop button exempts a flashing banner from Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A).
cards.explanation: Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A) limits flash frequency or demands staying below the general flash and red flash thresholds. A stop control does not establish safe flashing.
cards.misconception: A user-operated Stop control exempts flashing content from the flash-safety criterion.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.3.1: Three Flashes or Below Threshold

cards.statement: Animation from Interactions is a Level AA requirement for interface motion triggered by user actions.
cards.explanation: Animation from Interactions is Level AAA. It addresses disabling motion animation triggered by interaction, except when that animation is essential to the function or information.
cards.misconception: Disabling interaction-triggered motion animation is a Level AA requirement.

source.title: Understanding SC 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions

cards.statement: A bare `@media (prefers-reduced-motion)` query matches the same users as `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`.
cards.explanation: The reduce keyword evaluates as true and no-preference as false, so the bare media query targets only users who have asked for reduced motion.

source.title: prefers-reduced-motion CSS media feature - MDN Web Docs
